preamble: A velar ejective [kʼ] becomes a uvular implosive [ʛ]: the stop moves back to the uvula and the airstream switches from egressive to ingressive. Konso (Lowland East Cushitic) has no ejectives. Instead it has four implosives, ɓ ɗ ʄ ʛ. Orkaydo (2013: 8) states that ejectives in loanwords become implosives, and that Amharic kʼ systematically gives the uvular ʛ (also cʼ > ʄ, pʼ > ɓ, while tʼ and sʼ become plain t and s). Native Konso ʛ also continues Proto-East Cushitic *kʼ (Wikipedia's Proto-Cushitic table after Sasse 1979; examples below), while closely related Gidole keeps kʼ (Ehret 1991 #92). Separately, Ehret (1991) describes the Dullay and Yaaku reflex of PEC *kʼ, written q, as 'a uvular, but an unusual one, an implosive voiceless stop', i.e. [ʛ̥]. Burji and Gidole keep kʼ in some of the same roots (Ehret #92). The Konso loans have voiced ʛ, but the Dullay and Yaaku sound is voiceless, so the cell's voiced symbol fits it only approximately.
phoneticEffects: Implosivization, Retraction, Airstream Change, Loanword Adaptation

examples.note: Orkaydo (2013: 8). The final kʼ also becomes ʛ, and the initial cʼ becomes ʄ.

languageExamples.language: Proto-Eastern Cushitic to Dullay and Yaaku

examples.note: Ehret (1991) #92. Burji kʼooš- 'to peel' and Gidole kʼošš- 'to weed' keep kʼ.

examples.to: Yaaku -jaq-s- 'to throb, beat', Harso/Dobase/Gollango šoq- 'to hit', Saamakko joq- 'to strike'
Saamakko joq-om- 'to have diarrhoea', Dobase šoq-on-ko 'diarrhoea'

examples.note: Ehret (1991) #176. Hadiya qac-o 'soft' keeps kʼ (written q).

Orkaydo (2013: 33). Militarev (2005) gives Konso qanīn, Somali qanīn and Arbore ḳin(i)n-; StarLing writes the Konso consonant q where Orkaydo writes ʛ. Oromo ciniinuu 'to bite' (Wiktionary) has the ejective affricate c [tʃʼ] instead. The correspondence table in Wikipedia's Proto-Cushitic article, after Sasse (1979), gives ʛ as the regular Konso reflex of Proto-East Cushitic *kʼ, against kʼ in Oromo and Arbore.
Orkaydo (2013: 89). Oromo qalʔaa, qallaa keeps the ejective (Oromo q = [kʼ]) (Militarev 2005).

Orkaydo (2013: 9). Proto-form and cognates from Wiktionary (Waaq), after Sasse: Oromo Waaqa, Somali Waaq, Burji waac'i, Hadiya waa'a. Because Konso also turns borrowed kʼ into ʛ (Orkaydo 2013: 8), a loan from Oromo cannot be ruled out for this or any single item.
